content: Chronic spontaneous urticaria (CSU) is defined as the presence of hives, angioedema, or both for a duration of six weeks or longer. It is more common in adults than in children, and women are affected more frequently than men. The diagnosis of CSU is typically clinical, based on the episodic appearance of characteristic urticarial lesions, with or without angioedema, on most days of the week for at least six weeks. In 80 to 90 percent of cases, no specific cause can be identified. Routine skin biopsy is not required for diagnosis but may be performed to rule out urticarial vasculitis if there are signs of a vasculitic process or in rare cases with features of mastocytosis. Tests such as the autologous serum and plasma skin tests (ASST/APST), assays for autoantibodies against IgE or Fc-epsilon-RI, and in vitro assessments of basophil function are used in research to investigate the pathogenesis of CSU. However, these tests lack specificity, are not standardized, and are not recommended for routine clinical use. The most widely accepted hypothesis for the pathogenesis of CSU involves histamine-releasing factors and defects in basophil signaling or function, although the data supporting this are incomplete. CSU is a self-limiting condition in most patients. Spontaneous remission occurs in 30 to 50 percent of patients within one year, and the average disease duration is two to five years. However, up to 20 percent of patients may experience symptoms persisting beyond five years, with more severe cases tending to last longer. Patients with CSU often experience frustration and anxiety due to the chronic nature of the disease. While no external cause is identified in most cases, various factors can exacerbate the condition. Identifying and avoiding individual triggers is a critical part of management, and patient education should begin at the time of diagnosis. The first-line treatment for CSU is H1 antihistamines. Second-generation, less-sedating agents such as cetirizine, levocetirizine, fexofenadine, loratadine, and desloratadine are preferred over older first-generation agents like hydroxyzine, diphenhydramine, chlorpheniramine, or mizolastine due to their improved safety and tolerability profiles. Approximately 50 percent of patients may not achieve complete symptom control with standard doses of second-generation H1 antihistamines alone. For these non-responders, a stepwise approach to escalating therapy is recommended. This includes increasing the dose of the second-generation H1 antihistamine up to four times the standard dose. If symptoms persist, additional interventions may include adding a different second-generation antihistamine, an H2 antagonist, a leukotriene-receptor antagonist, or a first-generation H1 antihistamine at bedtime. For patients with refractory symptoms, systemic glucocorticoids may be used for short-term control, but their use should be limited due to potential side effects. Patients should be informed about the sedative and anticholinergic side effects of first-generation H1 antihistamines if these are used. Once symptoms are controlled, the medications required for symptom control should be continued for at least one to three months before attempting to taper or discontinue them. For patients with particularly difficult-to-control symptoms, the maintenance period may need to be extended. Andersen-Tawil syndrome (ATS), also known as Long QT syndrome 7, is a rare genetic disorder inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern. It is caused by mutations in the KCNJ2 or KCNJ5 genes. The KCNJ2 gene encodes the alpha subunit of the potassium channel Kir2.1, while the KCNJ5 gene encodes the G protein-activated inwardly rectifying potassium channel 4 (Kir3.4). ATS is characterized by a triad of features: ventricular arrhythmias, periodic paralysis or muscle weakness, and skeletal abnormalities such as micrognathia and clinodactyly. However, the clinical presentation can vary widely. The diagnosis of ATS is based on clinical findings, electrocardiographic (ECG) abnormalities, and genetic testing. Suggestive findings include periodic paralysis, symptomatic cardiac arrhythmias, or ECG evidence of prolonged QTc or QUc intervals, as well as characteristic facial and skeletal features. Genetic testing can confirm the diagnosis by identifying pathogenic variants in the KCNJ2 gene. Management of ATS requires a multidisciplinary approach involving neurologists and cardiologists. Treatment of periodic paralysis depends on serum potassium levels. For hypokalemic episodes, oral potassium supplementation is recommended, while hyperkalemic episodes may be managed with carbohydrate ingestion or mild exercise. Cardiac arrhythmias may require antiarrhythmic medications such as flecainide, which has been shown to reduce ventricular arrhythmias in ATS. Implantable cardioverter-defibrillators may be necessary for patients with tachycardia-induced syncope. Medications that prolong the QT interval or exacerbate hypokalemia should be avoided. Relatives at risk should undergo genetic testing or detailed neurologic and cardiologic evaluation to enable early diagnosis and treatment. The prognosis of ATS varies depending on the severity of cardiac and neuromuscular symptoms. With appropriate management, the risk of life-threatening complications can be significantly reduced.
